conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m <med>Dr. Maya Rivera</med>, a perinatal mental-health specialist. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you navigate these early weeks with your new baby.

Today I’ll be using a short tool called the <sym>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</sym>—or EPDS for short. It’s a set of ten questions we ask every new parent around this time, because the postpartum period can bring big emotional swings that are easy to overlook when you’re focused on your baby. The EPDS helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety early so we can offer the right help.

Everything you share is confidential and will stay between you and your care team. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear how you’ve really been feeling in the past seven days. We’ll go question by question, and I’ll keep the language simple and conversational. If any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I’ve noticed it’s gotten harder. I used to laugh more easily, but lately—even when my partner tries to be funny or I see something silly on my phone—I barely crack a smile. It feels like I’m too tired or just not in the mood most of the time.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish I could say that. I mean, every now and then something will make me chuckle, but it’s pretty rare. Mostly I just feel too worn-out or down to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of... flat. I’ll think “I should want to do this,” but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m not a good enough mom.” I’ll replay every little thing I did and convince myself it’s my fault, even when people tell me babies just cry sometimes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing—what if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking, what if the rash on her cheek is something awful, what if I’m missing some sign that she’s sick? I know it sounds extreme, but the worries just pop in even when everything’s actually fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah... it’s happened a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my heart starts pounding, and I feel like something terrible is about to happen—even when the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet. I’ll pace the hallway or grip the crib rail until the feeling finally passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the laundry, the bottles, the night feedings—they just pile up and I can’t quite catch my breath. Some mornings I’ll sit on the couch while she naps and think, “How am I going to get through everything?” I still do it all, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby’s finally down, my mind won’t settle. I lie there thinking I’m doing everything wrong, or I’ll hear her make a tiny sound and I’m wide-awake worrying. Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, and then I wake up at three or four and can’t get back to sleep because the same thoughts keep spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s how I feel most of the day. I get this heavy, sad feeling in my chest that just sits there. Sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and tears start rolling without any real reason. It’s like a cloud that follows me around, even when I try to remind myself I should be happy right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... I’ve cried—quietly, so no one would hear—three or four times this week. Once was after a diaper change, just because she wouldn’t stop squirming and I felt like I couldn’t even handle that. The tears come fast and hard, and afterward I feel drained and guilty for falling apart over “nothing.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby the way she deserves.

You've shared that over the past week laughter and anticipation feel almost out of reach, replaced by a persistent heavy sadness, daily worries about your baby's safety, and moments of panic that leave your chest tight and heart racing. Despite loving your little one and trying to keep everything afloat, you often blame yourself when things go wrong, cry easily over small frustrations, and lie awake ruminating long after the house is quiet.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports humor is rare and feels too worn-out or down to laugh, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure and describes anhedonia consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame, replaying events and taking full responsibility even when others reassure her, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries without cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic symptoms with chest tightness, racing heart, and dread occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm ('most days') and difficulty managing daily tasks, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption for 1-2 hours initially plus middle-of-night awakening, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week, triggered by minor stressors, consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 25 (range 0-30) exceeds the ≥13 threshold indicating probable major depression, with high scores on core depressive items (Q1,2,7,8,9) and co-occurring anxiety/panic (Q4,5). The patient describes <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>crying</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, and <sym>middle-insomnia</sym> nearly every day, consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No self-harm ideation was endorsed (Q10 = 0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
2. Ask about evidence-based options such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, peer support groups, and consider whether <med>antidepressant medication</med> might be appropriate for you
3. Share these EPDS results and your daily mood log with your partner or a trusted family member so they can help monitor changes and support appointments
4. Practice 10-15 minutes of gentle movement (stroller walk, stretching) and brief relaxation breathing when baby sleeps to reduce <sym>anxiety</sym> surges; keep expectations small and achievable
5. Plan a consistent bedtime routine: dim lights, hand off baby monitor to partner or support person for one scheduled 4-hour stretch, and limit screens to improve <sym>sleep onset</sym>
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress once treatment begins; if <sym>panic symptoms</sym> worsen or new urges to self-harm emerge, seek emergency care immediately
7. Access local resources: Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4773, National Maternal Mental Health hotline 1-833-943-5746, or community mother-and-baby support groups
8. Continue regular pediatric check-ups; inform your baby's healthcare provider about maternal mood so they can offer additional parenting support and developmental guidance
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: POSTPARTUM MOOD/ANXIETY SCREENING SUMMARY  
Date: [today]

Patient report (10-item EPDS-style query)

1. Anhedonia: marked reduction in capacity for laughter/pleasure; previously enjoyable activities feel “flat”  
2. Low mood: pervasive sadness, “heavy” feeling, daily tearfulness unrelated to situational triggers  
3. Excessive guilt/self-blame: recurrently attributes infant fussing to personal inadequacy; ruminates on perceived maternal failures  
4. Anxiety: daily, uncontrollable worries about infant safety; multiple episodes of panic (tight chest, racing heart) without objective danger  
5. Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep independent of infant needs; racing thoughts, heightened startle to baby sounds  
6. Functional impact: reports “treading water,” feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; no self-harm ideation expressed

Pattern: high endorsement of depressive symptoms (mood, anhedonia, guilt, crying, sleep) plus comorbid anxiety/panic; no safety concerns per Q10 response.

Screening significance: findings exceed threshold for probable major postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety; warrants formal clinical assessment with standardized tool (e.g., EPDS ≥13) and referral for appropriate perinatal mental health evaluation.
